health.title: Your recovery
health.disclaimer: General wellbeing information, not medical advice.
health.setback: Smoking pauses your recovery — but every fresh start counts. You've got this 💚

m_20min.title: Pulse & pressure
m_20min.body: Heart rate and blood pressure ease toward normal.
m_20min.detail: Within ~20 minutes of your last cigarette, the heart-rate and blood-pressure spike from nicotine starts settling toward your baseline.
m_20min.fact: Nicotine speeds your heart by ~10–20 beats per minute while you smoke.

m_30min.title: Warm hands
m_30min.body: Circulation reaches your fingers and toes again.
m_30min.detail: Nicotine narrows small blood vessels; as it fades, blood flows back to your hands and feet and they warm up.
m_30min.fact: Cold fingertips are a classic sign of a fresh cigarette.

m_1h.title: Nicotine clearing
m_1h.detail: Nicotine has a half-life of about one to two hours, so its level in your blood is already dropping.
m_1h.fact: By two hours, about half of it is already gone.

m_2h.title: First cravings
m_2h.body: Nicotine is half gone; cravings may knock.
m_2h.detail: As nicotine drops by roughly half, the first cravings tend to appear. Each one passes in a few minutes.
m_2h.fact: A craving rarely lasts longer than 3–5 minutes.

m_6h.title: Calmer rhythm
m_6h.detail: By about six hours nearly all the nicotine from your last cigarette has been metabolized and your heart rate and breathing are calmer.
m_6h.fact: Only ~3% of that nicotine remains after six hours.

m_8h.title: Oxygen rising
m_8h.body: Carbon monoxide halves; more oxygen flows.
m_8h.detail: Carbon monoxide takes oxygen’s place in your blood. Its level roughly halves by eight hours, so your blood carries more oxygen.
m_8h.fact: Carbon monoxide is the same gas that comes from a car’s exhaust.

m_12h.title: Blood near normal
m_12h.body: Carbon monoxide clears; blood oxygen normal.
m_12h.detail: By around twelve hours, carbon monoxide has largely cleared and your blood-oxygen level returns to normal.
m_12h.fact: More oxygen means less of that afternoon slump.

m_24h.title: Heart eases
m_24h.body: Heart-attack risk already starts to fall.
m_24h.detail: After a full day, the extra strain on your heart begins to lift and heart-attack risk starts to decline. Withdrawal can peak now — it passes.
m_24h.fact: Even one smoke-free day measurably lowers strain on your heart.

m_36h.title: Peak passing
m_36h.body: The loudest cravings start to fade.
m_36h.detail: Cravings and irritability tend to peak around a day and a half, then begin easing as your body adjusts.
m_36h.fact: This is often the toughest moment — and it’s downhill after.

m_48h.title: Taste & smell
m_48h.body: Nerve endings regrow; food comes alive.
m_48h.detail: Around 48 hours, nerve endings damaged by smoking start regrowing and your senses of taste and smell sharpen noticeably.
m_48h.fact: Many people say food ‘comes alive’ on day two.

m_72h.title: Easier breath
m_72h.detail: By about 72 hours the bronchial tubes relax, breathing feels easier and energy rises — and you’re now essentially nicotine-free.
m_72h.fact: Three days in, the physical addiction is largely behind you.

m_1week.title: One week strong
m_1week.body: The first week is hardest — and it’s done.
m_1week.detail: Most relapses happen in the first week, so reaching seven days is a real turning point. Cravings are already shorter and less frequent.
m_1week.fact: Make it past week one and your odds jump dramatically.

m_10day.title: Cravings shrink
m_10day.body: Urges are briefer and easier to ride out.
m_10day.detail: By about ten days, cravings are typically short — a few minutes — and come less often.
m_10day.fact: Each craving you ride out makes the next one weaker.

m_2week.title: Circulation
m_2week.body: Blood flows easier; moving feels lighter.
m_2week.detail: Around two weeks, circulation improves and lung function begins to climb, so walking and exercise feel easier. Gum blood flow nears a non-smoker’s.
m_2week.fact: Better circulation also helps cuts and gums heal.

m_3week.title: Real stamina
m_3week.body: Lung function rises; exercise gets easier.
m_3week.detail: By three weeks, measurable lung-function gains mean you can do more before getting winded.
m_3week.fact: Many people notice stairs are suddenly easier.

m_1month.title: Mind settles
m_1month.detail: Acute withdrawal — irritability, restlessness, low mood — largely settles within three to four weeks, and sleep often improves.
m_1month.fact: Cravings become occasional rather than constant.

m_6week.title: Healthier mouth
m_6week.detail: Within about six weeks, blood flow and healing in the gums improve, lowering the risk of gum disease.
m_6week.fact: Smokers heal from dental work noticeably slower.

m_2month.title: More energy
m_2month.detail: Around two months, stronger circulation and lung function show up as steadier energy and easier exercise.
m_2month.fact: Workouts that felt hard at week one feel routine now.

m_3month.title: Reward reset
m_3month.body: Lung function up; brain dopamine normalizes.
m_3month.detail: Lung function can be up 10–30%, and brain-imaging studies show the dopamine (reward) system returns to a non-smoker’s level by about three months.
m_3month.fact: A PET study found the smoking dopamine deficit fully normalized at 3 months.

m_4month.title: Clearer lungs
m_4month.detail: As airways heal and inflammation falls, coughing and wheezing keep declining through these months.
m_4month.fact: Your lungs are actively rebuilding their lining.

m_5month.title: Smoke feels foreign
m_5month.body: Cravings are rare; the habit loosens.
m_5month.detail: By around five months, cravings are infrequent and smoking starts to feel like something you used to do.
m_5month.fact: New smoke-free routines have largely taken over.

m_6month.title: Calm under stress
m_6month.body: You handle stress without a cigarette.
m_6month.detail: By six months many people cope with stress smoke-free, and coughing and mucus are much reduced.
m_6month.fact: Your go-to stress response is no longer nicotine.

m_9month.title: Lungs rebuilt
m_9month.detail: By about nine months the cilia have largely recovered, so your lungs clear mucus well and you catch fewer infections.
m_9month.fact: Cilia are your lungs’ tiny self-cleaning brushes.

m_1year.title: Stronger heart
m_1year.body: Heart-disease risk is about half a smoker’s.
m_1year.detail: One year smoke-free, your excess risk of coronary heart disease is about half that of someone who still smokes.
m_1year.fact: Your heart keeps getting safer every year from here.

m_18month.title: Steady and free
m_18month.detail: By a year and a half, smoke-free living is well established and your body keeps repairing quietly in the background.
m_18month.fact: Most ex-smokers say cravings are now rare surprises.

m_2year.title: Near-normal heart
m_2year.detail: Around two years, heart-attack risk continues dropping toward that of a never-smoker.
m_2year.fact: Two years is a milestone few relapse past.

m_5year.title: Lower stroke risk
m_5year.body: Stroke risk falls toward a never-smoker’s.
m_5year.detail: Within about five years, stroke risk drops substantially, and the risk of mouth, throat and esophagus cancers is roughly halved.
m_5year.fact: Blood vessels widen and clot less easily over these years.

m_10year.title: Lower cancer risk
m_10year.body: Lung-cancer death risk is about half a smoker’s.
m_10year.detail: By ten years, the risk of dying from lung cancer is roughly half that of someone who keeps smoking, and several other cancer risks fall too.
m_10year.fact: Risk of larynx and pancreatic cancer also drops.

m_15year.title: Heart like a non-smoker
m_15year.detail: After fifteen years, the risk of coronary heart disease is close to that of a person who never smoked.
m_15year.fact: Fifteen years undoes most cardiovascular risk.

m_20year.title: Full circle
m_20year.detail: By around twenty years, the risk of death from smoking-related causes approaches that of someone who never smoked.
m_20year.fact: Two decades on, your body has reclaimed most of the risk.
